questions.q: What is the side length of a square whose area is double that of a square with side 5 cm, according to Baudhayana's Sulba-Sutra method?
questions.a: The side length is the diagonal of the original 5 cm square, which is 5√2 cm (approximately 7.07 cm). A wrong answer of 10 cm reveals the student thinks doubling the side doubles the area (confusing linear and quadratic scaling). An answer of 7 cm without √2 suggests they measured but don't grasp the exact geometric relationship.

questions.q: Explain why using the diagonal of a square as the side of a new square exactly doubles the area, without using the formula a² + b² = c².
questions.a: The original square of side *a* can be split along its diagonal into two congruent right isosceles triangles. Four such triangles (two squares' worth) arrange perfectly around the diagonal to form a larger square whose side is the diagonal. Thus the new square comprises 4 triangles = 2 original squares. A wrong answer citing "Pythagoras theorem" shows reliance on later algebraic formalism instead of the Sulba-Sutra's visual area reasoning. An answer saying "diagonal is longer" without the triangle rearrangement misses the area-equivalence logic.

questions.q: A square courtyard has side 12 m. Using the Sulba-Sutra method, what is the area of the square constructed on its diagonal? Show your steps.
questions.a:
Step 1: Original square side = 12 m, area = 12² = 144 m².  
Step 2: Diagonal of original square becomes side of new square.  
Step 3: New square area = 2 × original area = 2 × 144 = 288 m².  
(Alternatively: diagonal = 12√2 m, new area = (12√2)² = 144 × 2 = 288 m².)  
A wrong answer of 576 m² (12² × 4) means the student doubled the side instead of the area. An answer of 144√2 m² confuses side length with area (forgetting to square the √2).

questions.q: Compare the Sulba-Sutra's "doubling a square" method with the modern formula for the diagonal of a square (d = a√2). What is the same and what is different in the underlying reasoning?
questions.a: Same: both recognise the diagonal as √2 times the side. Different: Sulba-Sutra uses constructive geometry (rope, area rearrangement) to *produce* the double-area square without ever computing √2 numerically; modern formula computes the diagonal length algebraically. A wrong answer saying "they are the same thing" misses the distinction between geometric construction (exact, operational) and algebraic computation (numerical approximation). An answer focusing only on √2 being irrational ignores the area-doubling purpose of the Sulba-Sutra.

questions.q: A student claims: "To double a square's area, just multiply the side by 1.5 because 1.5² = 2.25 which is close to 2." Evaluate this claim and explain why the Sulba-Sutra method is superior for exact construction.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect: 1.5² = 2.25 gives 12.5% excess area, not exact doubling. The Sulba-Sutra method using the diagonal gives *exact* doubling because (a√2)² = 2a² by geometric necessity — no approximation. A wrong evaluation accepting "close enough" reveals misunderstanding of the Sulba-Sutra's purpose: precise altar construction for rituals demanded exactness, not approximation. An answer saying "√2 ≈ 1.414 so 1.5 is wrong" uses decimal approximation rather than the exact geometric proof.

questions.q: Design a rope-and-stake procedure (like the Sulba-Sutra) to construct a square of area 50 m² starting from a square of area 25 m². Describe each step clearly so another student could follow it on a field.
questions.a:
1. Mark a square ABCD of side 5 m (area 25 m²) using stakes and rope.  
2. Stretch rope from A to C — this is the diagonal.  
3. With rope length AC fixed, mark point E such that AE = AC and ∠CAE = 90° (use 3-4-5 triangle or perpendicular bisector method).  
4. Similarly mark F, G to complete square AEFG with side = AC.  
5. Square AEFG has area 50 m².  
A poor answer that says "measure 7.07 m" uses decimal measurement, violating the Sulba-Sutra's exact constructive approach. An answer omitting the 90° angle construction misses the key geometric operation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______'s Sulba-Sutra describes a geometric method to construct a square with exactly twice the area of a given square: the side of the new square equals the diagonal of the original square.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a farmer in ______ India has a square field of side 10 metres and wants to mark out a new square field with exactly double the area for a different crop.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a farmer in ancient India has a square field of side ______ metres and wants to mark out a new square field with exactly double the area for a different crop.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why the diagonal of a square becomes the side of a square with double the area, describe the Sulba-Sutra's rope-based construction method, and connect this geometric relationship to the irrational number √2 without relying on algebraic formula memorization.
